proposed_features.description: Groups education into broad tiers (basic, vocational, professional, advanced) to capture the strong correlation between higher education and higher income brackets.
Distinguishes between manual/labor-intensive roles and professional/managerial roles, which typically command higher salaries.
Indicates whether the individual has reported capital gains, a strong indicator of investment income which often correlates with higher total earnings.
Categorizes weekly working hours to distinguish part-time, standard, and overtime work patterns, which can influence total income.
Combines marital status and relationship to identify household structure, as married individuals often have higher reported household income or different employment stability.
Segments age into career stages (early, mid, late) to capture the typical income trajectory over a lifetime.
Differentiates between private sector, self-employment, and government work, as self-employment and certain government roles can have different income distributions.
Captures demographic factors that may correlate with income disparities in the dataset, serving as a proxy for socioeconomic background.
Accounts for gender-based income differences that may exist in the dataset, particularly in certain occupations or education levels.
Distinguishes between native-born and foreign-born individuals, as immigration status and country of origin can influence income levels and job types.
Uses the final weight as a proxy for the representativeness of the record; higher weights might indicate more stable or common demographic profiles.
Evaluates whether the education level is consistent with the occupation (e.g., Masters with Prof-specialty), indicating human capital utilization which affects income.
Checks for the presence of multiple income sources (wages + capital gains/losses), which often indicates higher financial stability and total income.
